headline: This vendor draft does not back up the Zephyr MSA: Tarang would own the labelled data AtliQ must hand to the Client, answers for delay only if wilful while AtliQ answers without a cap, and has no duty to report a data breach. AtliQ can end in 7 days but Tarang needs 60, and AtliQ's own payment terms are longer than the ones Karandeep refused at PixelCraft.

findings.title: Tarang owns the labelled dataset AtliQ must deliver to the Client
findings.quote: The Vendor owns all labelled datasets, scripts and other outputs of the Services (the "Outputs").
findings.explanation: Milestone 1 of the Client MSA is 'Data foundation and labelled customer dataset', and the Client MSA says Deliverables become the Client's property on payment. Under this draft AtliQ only gets a non-exclusive, non-transferable licence to use the Outputs for the End Client Project, so it cannot pass ownership to the Client. Karandeep's rule is that the client owns what AtliQ builds for it. A similar vendor-owns-IP term at Rohan Iyer was waved through; that is a pattern to stop, not a precedent for this deal.

findings.title: Customer personal data sits with Tarang with no breach notice, no instructions clause and the Client's terms not passed down
findings.quote: AtliQ will provide the Vendor with extracts of the end client's customer transaction data for labelling, including customer names and mobile numbers.
findings.explanation: The Client MSA requires DPDP compliance, processing only on the Client's instructions and notice within 48 hours of a breach. This draft has none of those duties, lets Tarang store the data on its own systems and use its own contractors, and keeps confidentiality for 2 years against 5 in the Client MSA. If Tarang has a breach, AtliQ cannot meet its own 48-hour duty because Tarang has no duty to tell it. Rule R-16 asks for approval and flow-down before a subcontractor touches personal data.

findings.title: Delay and liability do not match the Client MSA: Tarang answers only for wilful delay, AtliQ answers without a cap
findings.quote: The Vendor shall be liable for delay only where the delay is caused by the Vendor's wilful default.
findings.explanation: The Client MSA makes AtliQ indemnify the Client for delay 'howsoever caused', expressly including delay by its subcontractors, with no cap. Tarang's delivery duty is 'reasonable efforts', it is liable for delay only if wilful, and its total liability is capped at the fees paid to it. If Tarang is late, the Client can claim against AtliQ without limit and AtliQ has almost nothing to recover. Tarang can also leave on 60 days' notice (§8.2) while AtliQ stays bound to M1. This is the gap the Zephyr brief's F-02 creates; see that brief for the rule position.

findings.title: AtliQ can end in 7 days but Tarang, an 8-person firm, must give 60; pay is only for accepted deliverables
findings.quote: AtliQ may terminate this Agreement for convenience on seven (7) days' written notice, and shall pay only for deliverables it has accepted before the termination date.
findings.explanation: Rule R-20 flags one-sided termination periods against a small vendor in AtliQ's own paper, and the checklist says that on termination the other side is paid for work done. Karandeep softened PixelCraft's paper for the same reason: 'They're six people.' Tarang is described in this draft as having eight people.

findings.title: Pay-when-paid with a 90-day long-stop is longer than the terms Karandeep refused at PixelCraft
findings.quote: AtliQ shall pay each invoice within thirty (30) days after AtliQ receives the corresponding payment from the end client, and in any event within ninety (90) days after receipt of the invoice.
findings.explanation: Rule R-05 tests pay-when-paid in AtliQ's own paper against the same limit: 30 days, 45 at most. Here the Vendor may wait up to 90 days. At PixelCraft, Karandeep deleted a 60-day payment term and set 30 days.
